ramx-01-c1.text: John Hayward (Gazetteer of the United States of America, 1854), quoted by House Divided, Dickinson College (1854). Rochester, New York (Hayward). House Divided: The Civil War Research Engine, Dickinson College.
ramx-01-c1.claim: Rochester grew from about 1,500 people in 1820 to about 9,000 in 1830

ramx-06-c2.quote: In her quest for health, she had visited Dr. Phineas P. Quimby of Portland, Maine, in 1862, and found that his nonmedical principles cured her.
ramx-06-c2.claim: From 1862 she was treated by, and studied with, Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, a mental healer in Portland, Maine.

ramx-02-c1.quote: Ann, like the majority of children of her class and time, received no formal schooling (she would, in fact, remain illiterate her entire life) and went to work at the burgeoning textile mills at age eight.
ramx-02-c1.claim: Ann Lee (1736 to 1784), an illiterate blacksmith's daughter from Manchester who had worked in a cotton mill, joined the group in 1758.

ramx-03-c2.quote: In 1869, when Oneida was on firmer financial ground, Noyes embarked on a program of stirpiculture, encouraging the most nearly perfect among the community to become parents.
ramx-03-c2.claim: In 1869 Noyes launched stirpiculture, from Latin stirps, "stock" or "root": a program of planned human breeding.

ramx-03-c1.quote: By 1875 approximately three hundred people lived in the community.
ramx-03-c1.claim: The Oneida Community grew to about 300 members, with a smaller branch at Wallingford, Connecticut.

ramx-03-c3.quote: In January 1881 each former Oneidan received shares of stock in Oneida, Ltd. (capitalized at $600,000), which has since become a silverware manufacturer.
ramx-03-c3.claim: On January 1, 1881, the community reorganized as a joint-stock company, Oneida Community, Limited, with members receiving shares in place of common property.

ramx-04-c1.quote: In 1832 a part of the colony, under "Count Leon," a German adventurer, withdrew to form a separate community.
ramx-04-c1.claim: In 1832 a newcomer calling himself "Count de Leon," Bernhard Müller, claimed prophetic authority and split the community

ramx-04-c3.text: Brook Farm. Gale Encyclopedia of U.S. Economic History.
ramx-04-c3.quote: It was established in 1841 by Unitarian minister and author George Ripley (1802 – 80), a leader of the Transcendental movement.
ramx-04-c3.claim: Brook Farm, at West Roxbury near Boston, was founded in 1841 by George Ripley, a former Unitarian minister

ramx-05-c2.text: Serpent Handling. e-WV: The West Virginia Encyclopedia.
ramx-05-c2.quote: West Virginia is the only state that legally permits serpent handling.
ramx-05-c2.claim: West Virginia never passed a ban, and handling remains legal there.
